entities.name: Bartolo di Fredi
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Bartolo di Fredi, also known as Bartolo Battiloro, was a prominent Italian painter of the Sienese School, active from the mid-14th century until his death in 1410. Emerging in the wake of the devastating Black Death, which profoundly impacted Sienese artistic traditions, Bartolo played a crucial role in revitalizing and transmitting the distinctive, expressive style of Siena's Trecento masters. His career spanned a period of significant social and religious change, during which he became a leading figure, known for his prolific output of altarpieces, frescoes, and smaller devotional works that catered to both ecclesiastical and private patrons across Tuscany.

His artistic achievements include major fresco cycles depicting Old Testament scenes in the Collegiata di San Gimignano (circa 1356), a monumental undertaking that showcased his narrative skill and compositional ambition. Among his most celebrated altarpieces are the *Adoration of the Magi* (1385, Siena Pinacoteca), a vibrant and richly detailed work, and the *Coronation of the Virgin* (1388, Montalcino, Museo Civico), both demonstrating his characteristic use of bright colors, elongated figures, and an emphasis on lyrical storytelling. Bartolo maintained a highly successful workshop in Siena, producing numerous commissions for churches, confraternities, and civic bodies, cementing his status as one of the most sought-after artists of his time.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bartolo di Fredi played a pivotal role in sustaining and evolving the distinctive Sienese painting tradition during the late Trecento, bridging the styles of earlier masters with future generations. His prolific output of altarpieces and fresco cycles across Tuscany significantly shaped the visual and religious culture of the region, ensuring the continuity of a unique aesthetic.
